strengths: The paper has a clear and appealing motivation: using self-supervised visuomotor prediction to learn an agent/body representation without privileged robot masks, addressing a real limitation of prior agent-environment disentanglement methods such as SEAR.

The proposed Ego-Foresight architecture is conceptually simple and well aligned with the robotics setting: visual context plus proprioceptive/motor information predicts future robot appearance, with a similarity loss encouraging scene information to be separated from agent motion.

The empirical section includes both a real-world video prediction dataset and simulated manipulation tasks, and compares against relevant image-based RL baselines including DrQ-v2 and the closely related supervised SEAR method.

The reported Meta-world results are promising on several tasks, with improvements in final success rate and sample efficiency over the baselines, and the paper provides useful implementation details, hyperparameters, compute information, and some ablations over prediction horizon and auxiliary-loss weight.
weaknesses: There is a potentially serious technical ambiguity in the RL integration. The paper states that the actor and critic receive the concatenation of hs and hp, but hp is defined as encoding a sequence of future proprioceptive states. It is unclear what information is available at action-selection time, and whether the RL agent is inadvertently given future trajectory/proprioceptive information from replay. If so, the evaluation would be invalid; if not, the method description needs to be much more precise.

The experimental evidence for the representation-learning claim on BAIR is mostly qualitative. The paper shows a few examples but lacks quantitative prediction/disentanglement metrics, systematic evaluation on held-out motions, comparisons to video prediction or disentanglement baselines, or evidence that moving objects are consistently ignored while robot motion is captured.

The RL evaluation is limited in statistical strength. Only 3 seeds are used for an unstable DDPG-based setting, and the paper reports ranges rather than confidence intervals or significance tests. Several tasks show weak or mixed results, and the claimed average gains may be sensitive to the aggregation rule and task selection.

The baseline set is too narrow for a top-tier RL/robot learning paper. DrQ-v2 and SEAR are relevant, but the paper does not compare to other auxiliary prediction/objective methods, model-based approaches, proprioception-augmented policies, or simpler controls that would isolate whether gains come from the proposed disentanglement mechanism rather than extra proprioceptive input, auxiliary reconstruction, architecture size, or motor babbling.

Important ablations are missing or underdeveloped: no clear ablation of the similarity loss, proprioception encoder, future versus current proprioception, motor-babbling duration, reconstruction loss alone, feature dimensionality/capacity, pretraining versus joint training, or whether the method still helps when baselines receive comparable proprioceptive information and compute.

The sample-efficiency analysis is not fully convincing. Ego-Foresight requires a 50k-step motor-babbling phase, and the definition of sample efficiency as time to 90% of the best model’s performance with NA handling can bias averages. The paper should report clearer area-under-curve or fixed-budget metrics with uncertainty.

The method’s practical scope remains narrow: all main control experiments use simulated Sawyer Meta-world tasks, while the real-world component is only offline prediction. Claims about adapting to changing body schemas or tool use are intriguing but not directly evaluated beyond qualitative observations.

Reproducibility is only partial at submission time because the code is promised for later release. Some architectural details are also confusing or contain apparent typos, which makes independent reproduction harder than the checklist suggests.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful problem: improving sample efficiency in visual reinforcement learning by learning an unsupervised agent/self representation rather than relying on simulator masks or CAD-based supervision.

The proposed Ego-Foresight idea is intuitive and reasonably well motivated by motor prediction: conditioning future visual prediction on proprioception provides a plausible route to separating controllable agent motion from the rest of the scene.

The paper evaluates both on a real robot video dataset (BAIR) for qualitative visuomotor prediction and on 10 Meta-world manipulation tasks, including comparison to DrQ-v2 and SEAR, which are relevant baselines for this setting.
The method is relatively simple to implement on top of image-based DDPG/DrQ-style pipelines, and the appendix provides many hyperparameters and architectural details.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too thin for the strength of the claims. The main RL results use only 3 random seeds despite the paper itself emphasizing DDPG instability, and the shaded regions are only best/worst ranges. There are no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or enough seeds to support claims of consistent 23% efficiency and 8% performance improvement.

The comparison is potentially confounded by the required 50k-step motor-babbling stage and by architectural/training differences. It is unclear whether the gains come from the proposed self-prediction regularizer, additional exploration data, altered representation capacity, auxiliary reconstruction training, or other implementation choices.

The ablations are insufficient. The paper varies beta and prediction horizon on a fixed task, but does not isolate the similarity loss, reconstruction-only variants, proprioception-only/visual-only variants, pretraining versus joint training, motor-babbling length, or capacity-matched auxiliary losses. This makes the mechanism behind the reported gains largely unproven.

The real-world BAIR evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. Claims about disentangling agent and environment, predicting unseen trajectories, and ignoring moving objects are supported by a few visual examples rather than quantitative segmentation, prediction, controllability, or generalization metrics.

The strongest claimed novelty is limited. The method combines known components: video prediction/reconstruction, slow-feature-style scene consistency, proprioceptive conditioning, and an auxiliary RL loss. The paper does not convincingly distinguish its contribution from prior agent/environment disentanglement, robot-awareness, or auxiliary predictive representation methods beyond removing mask supervision.

The Meta-world benchmark scope is narrow for a top-tier AI contribution: 10 single-task manipulation settings, all with a Sawyer embodiment, no real-world control experiments, no cross-robot transfer, no multi-task learning, and no direct test of the claimed adaptation to tools except qualitative interpretation of a hammer example.

Sample-efficiency accounting is not fully convincing. The paper defines efficiency relative to 90% of the best model's performance and assigns the final plotted step when a method fails to reach that threshold, which can bias aggregate efficiency summaries and obscure failure modes such as Bin Picking and Assembly where all methods are weak.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although many hyperparameters are listed, there is no clear code release statement, and important details such as exact task variants, camera settings, action/state preprocessing, evaluation protocol details, and compute-budget parity across methods remain under-specified.

Some claims are overstated or speculative, especially about unsupervised awareness of self, body-schema adaptation, tool incorporation, and model-based planning applicability. These ideas are interesting, but the experiments do not provide strong evidence for them.

The paper contains presentation issues and minor errors that reduce polish, including awkward wording, a dangling footnote marker near the contribution list, and occasional unclear notation such as the decoder input size being described as the sum of hs and hs rather than hs and hp.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and relevant problem in visual robotic RL: improving sample efficiency by separating agent-related visual dynamics from environment dynamics without requiring supervised robot masks.

The proposed Ego-Foresight objective is conceptually appealing and well motivated: predicting future robot appearance from context frames and proprioceptive trajectories is a natural self-supervised signal for learning a self/body representation.

The method is evaluated both on a real-world robotic interaction dataset for visuomotor prediction and on 10 Meta-world manipulation tasks for downstream RL, which gives the paper a broader empirical base than a single benchmark result.

The RL comparisons include strong and relevant baselines, especially DrQ-v2 and SEAR, the latter being a close supervised disentanglement baseline. The reported gains over SEAR on several tasks are encouraging because Ego-Foresight removes the need for mask supervision.

The paper provides useful implementation detail, including architectures, hyperparameters, seeds, compute requirements, and training protocols, which makes the work relatively reproducible if the promised code is released.
The results are presented with per-task learning curves and ranges over seeds, making it possible to see where the method is clearly beneficial, comparable, or worse than baselines.
weaknesses: The empirical support is promising but not fully decisive. The main RL experiments use only 3 random seeds, which is low for unstable image-based DDPG-style training, and the paper does not report statistical tests or confidence intervals for the claimed average improvements.

The BAIR evaluation is almost entirely qualitative. The paper claims disentanglement, ignored object motion, and generalization to unseen trajectories, but provides only a few visual examples and no quantitative metrics, controlled tests, or systematic comparison to video prediction/disentanglement alternatives.

The ablation study is too narrow. The effects of prediction horizon and beta are shown on a single task, but there are no clear ablations for the similarity loss, proprioception encoder, motor-babbling stage, architecture choices, feature dimensionality, or using the auxiliary prediction loss without the proposed disentanglement structure.

The sample-efficiency comparison is somewhat fragile. Ego-Foresight includes a 50k-step motor-babbling phase, and the paper’s efficiency metric uses time to reach 90% of the best model with special handling for runs that never reach that threshold. This makes the reported 23% average efficiency improvement sensitive to metric design and task selection.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The discussion of body-schema adaptation and tool incorporation is interesting, but only weakly supported by qualitative hammer examples rather than targeted experiments on morphology changes, tool use, or transfer.

The method’s novelty is moderate rather than high. It combines known ingredients: video representation disentanglement, proprioceptive-conditioned prediction, auxiliary reconstruction losses for RL, and SEAR-style agent/environment separation. The self-supervised replacement for masks is useful, but the technical mechanism is relatively straightforward.

Fairness of comparison could be clearer. Ego-Foresight uses additional losses, proprioceptive future information, motor babbling, and possibly different representational capacity than the baselines; the paper does not fully isolate which of these factors accounts for the gains.

The paper acknowledges that hyperparameters were not optimized due to compute constraints, but this cuts both ways: the method may improve with tuning, yet the current comparison may also reflect suboptimal baseline or task-specific choices.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and intuitive self-supervised mechanism for learning agent-aware visual representations through visuomotor prediction, removing the explicit agent-mask supervision required by the closest baseline, SEAR.

The method is technically simple and reasonably well motivated: splitting latent features into scene and agent components, using a bottleneck plus action-conditioned rollout, and training the auxiliary reconstruction objective jointly with DrQ-v2 is easy to understand and potentially reusable.

The experimental scope is nontrivial, with results over 25 simulated RL tasks, 5 seeds, comparisons to DrQ-v2, supervised SEAR, and Dreamer-v3, plus qualitative experiments on real-world BAIR robot videos.

The method shows meaningful gains over DrQ-v2 on many Meta-World tasks and appears especially promising on tool-use tasks, where the learned representation can include held tools as part of the controllable body schema.

The paper is generally readable, well positioned against agent-environment disentanglement and model-based RL work, and includes ablations over key introduced hyperparameters such as auxiliary-loss weight, horizon, bottleneck size, and babbling length.
weaknesses: The central disentanglement claim is not quantitatively validated. Evidence for agent-awareness mainly comes from gradient visualizations and qualitative reconstructions; there are no segmentation metrics, controllability metrics, mutual-information analyses, or systematic tests showing that ha contains agent/tool information while hs excludes it.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The work combines known ingredients: auxiliary prediction losses, action-conditioned video/latent prediction, bottlenecked representation learning, motor babbling, and DrQ-v2-style visual RL. The main distinction from supervised agent-representation work is the self-supervised loss, but the paper does not sharply establish why this mechanism is fundamentally new or superior beyond empirical convenience.

The RL evidence is mixed. Ego-Foresight improves DrQ-v2 on 17/25 tasks, but performs poorly on the Distracting DMC benchmark and is often clearly below Dreamer-v3. Some claimed competitiveness with Dreamer-v3 is therefore overstated, especially since Dreamer-v3 dominates many DMC plots.

The comparison may not be fully fair or diagnostic. The method uses additional architectural components, an auxiliary decoder, an initial 25k-step motor-babbling phase, and tuned hyperparameters, while the baselines are mostly run with defaults. It is unclear whether gains come from agent-aware disentanglement specifically, from extra random exploration, from regularization, from larger capacity, or from reconstruction pretext learning.

The aggregate metric is unusual and potentially favorable to the proposed method: measuring performance at the step where any baseline reaches 85/90/95% of the maximum achieved by any method is hard to interpret and may obscure asymptotic or per-task failures. Standard area-under-curve, fixed-budget, final-performance, and statistical significance comparisons would be more convincing.

The real-world component is only qualitative and does not demonstrate real-world control, adaptation speed, or downstream improvement. The claim that the method is a step toward real-world model-free RL is plausible but not directly supported by real-world RL experiments.
The ablation study appears limited to a single Meta-World Door Open task, which is insufficient for conclusions about the method’s design choices across the diverse settings where it is evaluated.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: exact training budgets, wall-clock overhead, architecture sizes for all components, hyperparameter selection protocol, environment/task list, and code availability are not sufficiently specified for confident independent replication.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving sample efficiency for pixel-based RL by learning agent-aware representations without simulator-provided masks.

The proposed Ego-Foresight objective is conceptually simple and plausibly useful: action-conditioned prediction with a bottlenecked agent feature subspace is a reasonable self-supervised way to bias representations toward controllable body motion.
The evaluation includes relevant baselines, especially DrQ-v2 and the supervised SEAR method, and reports results over a reasonably broad set of simulated robotics tasks with multiple seeds.

The paper includes some ablations over the introduced hyperparameters and acknowledges important limitations such as sensitivity to distractors, the fixed motor-babbling phase, and additional wall-clock cost.
weaknesses: The central claims about agent-environment disentanglement are not convincingly established. Most evidence is qualitative visualization, a few prediction examples, and gradient-based saliency; there is no quantitative measure of disentanglement, controllability, mask quality, object/agent separation, or robustness to confounded action-object motion.

The novelty is limited relative to prior work on auxiliary prediction losses, action-conditioned video prediction, controllable representation learning, and supervised agent/environment disentanglement such as SEAR. The paper mainly replaces mask supervision with a reconstruction bottleneck and motor babbling, but does not sufficiently distinguish this from standard self-supervised dynamics/representation objectives.

The real-world component is weak: BAIR is used only for qualitative prediction examples, with no real-world control experiment, no quantitative prediction metrics, and only a single handcrafted unseen trajectory example. This does not substantiate the stronger claims about real-world transferability or model-based planning applicability.

The RL evidence is mixed and somewhat overclaimed. Ego-Foresight improves DrQ-v2 on 17/25 tasks, but underperforms badly on several distracting-background tasks and is not consistently competitive with Dreamer-v3. The aggregate metric is nonstandard and potentially favorable, and the paper does not provide statistical significance tests or enough detail to assess whether gains are robust.

The ablation study is too narrow, apparently focused on a single Meta-World Door Open task. Key design choices are not isolated adequately, including the role of motor babbling versus the representation loss, reconstruction versus alternatives, bottleneck size across domains, skip connections, pretraining versus joint training, and compute-normalized comparisons.

Fairness of comparison is unclear. The method introduces extra data collection behavior through a 25k-step random babbling phase, extra model components, and additional training losses, but the paper does not clearly normalize for wall-clock time, compute, environment interaction budget, or hyperparameter tuning effort across baselines.

The method has an important failure mode exactly in visually rich/distracting settings, where self-supervised reconstruction can force encoding of task-irrelevant details. This is a serious limitation for the claimed path toward real-world visual RL, and the proposed solution is deferred to future work.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence, especially tool incorporation into body schema, adaptation to changing embodiments, generalization to imagined trajectories, and applicability to model-based planning. These are interesting hypotheses but are not demonstrated with rigorous experiments.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission: the paper does not specify enough implementation, tuning, compute, architecture, and training protocol details to confidently reproduce the results from the main text alone.

The writing is generally understandable but contains presentation issues, typos, and occasional imprecise wording; more importantly, the narrative leans on neuroscience motivation while the actual technical contribution and empirical validation remain comparatively modest.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and appealing self-supervised mechanism for learning agent-aware visual representations: using action-conditioned prediction with an agent-feature bottleneck to separate predictable self-motion from the rest of the scene. This is well motivated relative to prior supervised mask-based approaches such as SEAR.

The empirical RL evaluation is reasonably broad for this area, covering 25 tasks across Meta-World, Distracting DMC, and Hurdle DMC, with 5 seeds and comparisons to DrQ-v2, supervised SEAR, and Dreamer-v3. The results show meaningful gains over DrQ-v2 on many tasks, especially manipulation/tool-use tasks, and competitiveness with stronger baselines in several settings.
The method is simple to integrate into an existing pixel-based model-free RL algorithm as an auxiliary representation-learning objective, which increases its practical relevance.

The paper includes useful qualitative evidence on simulated and BAIR real-world robotic data, showing that the learned predictor often tracks robot motion while leaving external moving objects comparatively static, and that tool motion can become incorporated into the learned agent representation.
The ablations over auxiliary-loss weight, prediction horizon, agent-feature dimension, and motor-babbling duration are helpful and identify several important design choices.
weaknesses: The evidence for agent-environment disentanglement is mostly qualitative. Gradient visualizations and a small number of reconstructions are suggestive, but the paper lacks quantitative segmentation, controllability, or representation-probing metrics that would more directly support the central disentanglement claim.

The real-world component is limited to qualitative prediction on an offline BAIR dataset. The paper does not demonstrate improved policy learning or control on real robots, so the claims about steps toward real-world model-free RL remain somewhat aspirational.

The RL gains are mixed: Ego-Foresight improves many tasks but underperforms or provides limited benefit on Distracting DMC, and Dreamer-v3 remains clearly stronger on several tasks. This weakens the broad claim that the approach generally improves sample efficiency and performance.

The ablation study appears to be conducted on a single Meta-World task, which limits confidence that the chosen hyperparameters and design conclusions transfer across domains, especially given the observed sensitivity on Distracting DMC.

The aggregate metric based on reaching fractions of the best baseline's maximum performance is somewhat nonstandard and could obscure per-task failures or variance. More conventional summary statistics, statistical tests, or area-under-curve comparisons would make the empirical case stronger.

The method introduces extra wall-clock cost and a motor-babbling phase, but the paper does not quantify computational overhead or analyze the tradeoff between added training cost and environment-sample savings in enough detail.

Some implementation and reproducibility details are underspecified in the main text, including full hyperparameter choices for all domains, exact architecture sizes, tuning protocol for baselines, and whether code/checkpoints will be released.
